# Categorical predictors

<style>
  :root {
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` mantis shrimp have 12 types of [photoreceptor]{.hl} for colour in their eyes. Humans have three.

_Source: Thoen et al. (2014), Science_
:::

## Today

- What a categorical predictor is, and how R stores it: factors
- Treatment coding: the default in R
- Dummy coding by hand, and changing the reference level
- Sum coding
- Predictors with more than two levels
- Combining categorical and continuous predictors

## So far

Until now every predictor was a number: frequency, length, age of acquisition. Each slope was a change in `y` per unit of `x`.

. . .

Many linguistic predictors are categories instead: voicing (voiced, voiceless), speaking style (casual, clear, loud), language, condition, speaker group, word class.

. . .

What does "one unit more" mean for `voicing`?

## The data

Vowels are longer before [voiced]{.hl} consonants (_bead_) than before [voiceless]{.hl} ones (_beat_). `vowel_voicing` is a production study with 60 vowels of each kind, duration in ms:

```{r}
vowels <- vowel_voicing
vowels |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), sd = sd(duration), n = n(), .by = voicing)
```

## The data

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.4
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = voicing, y = duration, colour = voicing)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 6, shape = 18, colour = mist) +
  labs(x = "Following consonant", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

White: the mean of each group. A model with voicing as a predictor should recover these two means.

# Treatment coding

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` mantis shrimp come in two kinds: [smashers]{.hl} break open crabs, clams and snails with club-like limbs, and spearers ambush fish from their burrows and impale them.

_Source: UC Berkeley News_
:::

## `lm()` with a categorical predictor {.smaller}

```{r}
m <- lm(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)
coef(m)
```

. . .

Compare with the group means:

```{r}
vowels |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = voicing)
```

. . .

- The intercept is the mean of `voiceless`
- The slope `voicingvoiced` is the difference between the two, voiced minus voiceless

## The reference level {.smaller}

Why is `voiceless` the intercept? As in lecture 1, R stores categories as a factor, a variable with a fixed set of levels in a fixed order:

```{r}
levels(vowels$voicing)
```

. . .

The first level becomes the [reference level]{.hl}, and every other level is compared against it. R names the coefficient `voicingvoiced`: the predictor, then the level being compared with the reference.

. . .

When R turns text into a factor itself, it puts the levels in alphabetical order (lecture 1), and `voiced` would come first:

```{r}
levels(factor(as.character(vowels$voicing)))
```

## Treatment coding, visually

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
means <- vowels |> summarise(duration = mean(duration), .by = voicing) |>
  mutate(x = if_else(voicing == "voiceless", 0, 1))

vowels |>
  mutate(x = if_else(voicing == "voiceless", 0, 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = duration)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = voicing), width = 0.06, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +
  geom_line(data = means, colour = mist, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = means, colour = mist, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.08, y = means$duration[means$x == 0] - 10, hjust = 0, colour = mist, size = 5,
           label = "intercept = mean of voiceless") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.45, y = mean(means$duration) + 14, hjust = 1, colour = hornbill, size = 5,
           label = paste("slope =", round(means$duration[means$x == 1] - means$duration[means$x == 0], 1), "ms")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("voiceless\n(0)", "voiced\n(1)"),
                     limits = c(-0.25, 1.25)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

In [treatment coding]{.hl}, the reference level is 0 and the other level is 1, so the regression line goes through the two means. A one-unit change in x is the change from one category to the other.

## Dummy coding by hand

This is exactly what R does behind the scenes:

```{r}
vowels <- vowels |>
  mutate(voiced01 = if_else(voicing == "voiced", 1, 0))

coef(lm(duration ~ voiced01, data = vowels))
```

. . .

The numbers are the same as before. A variable coded 0 and 1 like this is called a [dummy variable]{.hl}.

## Changing the reference level {.smaller}

To compare with voiced vowels instead, set the order of the levels with `fct_relevel()` from `{forcats}`:

```{r}
vowels_voiced <- vowels |>
  mutate(voicing = fct_relevel(voicing, "voiced"))

levels(vowels_voiced$voicing)
coef(lm(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels_voiced))
```

. . .

The intercept is now the `voiced` mean, and the slope is `r round(-diff(tapply(vowels$duration, vowels$voicing, mean)))` ms for voiceless. The model and its fit are unchanged; only the comparison is different.

## Choosing the reference level

- Choose the level that makes the coefficients easiest to read. This is often a natural baseline, such as a control condition or the standard variety, or else the most frequent category
- Set it explicitly, rather than relying on the alphabet

. . .

In R, the reference level of a factor is simply its first level.

## Discussion

Your study compares L1 English speakers with three groups of L2 speakers of English, whose first languages are German, Italian and Mandarin.

- Which group would you choose as the reference level, and why?
- Would your choice change if your question were about differences among the three L2 groups?

# Sum coding

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the [peacock mantis shrimp]{.hl} strikes snail shells at up to 23 m/s (about 83 km/h), with accelerations of up to 8,000 times gravity. The strike also makes bubbles that collapse with destructive force.

_Sources: Patek, Korff & Caldwell (2004), Nature; UC Berkeley News_
:::

## Sum coding

[Sum coding]{.hl} codes the two levels as +1 and −1, instead of 0 and 1:

```{r}
contrasts(vowels$voicing) <- contr.sum(2)
contrasts(vowels$voicing)
```

. . .

```{r}
coef(lm(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels))
```

## Reading sum-coded coefficients

```{r}
means <- vowels |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = voicing)
mean(means$mean)
diff(means$mean) / 2
```

. . .

The mean of the two group means, and half their difference.

- The intercept is the [grand mean]{.hl}, the average of the group means
- The coefficient is how far each group lies from that grand mean, with `+` for the first level and `−` for the second

## Sum coding, visually

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
grand <- mean(means$mean)
ggplot(vowels, aes(x = voicing, y = duration, colour = voicing)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = grand, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(data = means, aes(x = voicing, xend = voicing, y = grand, yend = mean),
               colour = mist, linewidth = 1.2,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(data = means, aes(y = mean), colour = mist, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = grand + 4, label = "grand mean = intercept",
           colour = mist, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Following consonant", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Arrows: the sum-coded coefficient, `±` `r round(abs(diff(means$mean)) / 2, 1)` ms from the grand mean.

## Treatment or sum coding?

| | Treatment (0 / 1) | Sum (+1 / −1) |
|---|---|---|
| Intercept | mean of the reference level | grand mean |
| Coefficient | difference from the reference | deviation from the grand mean |
| Default in R | yes | no: `contr.sum()` |

. . .

The fit is identical. The choice changes what the intercept means, which matters most when you add interactions (next week).

# More than two levels

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` despite their 12 receptors, mantis shrimp were worse than humans, bees and butterflies at [telling similar colours apart]{.hl}. They seem to encode colour unlike any other animal studied: perhaps by recognising colours rather than comparing them.

_Sources: Thoen et al. (2014), Science; Sci.News_
:::

## Speaking style

`speech_styles`: vowel duration in three speaking styles, 50 vowels each:

```{r}
styles <- speech_styles
styles |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = style)
```

## Speaking style

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.4
ggplot(styles, aes(x = style, y = duration, colour = style)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 6, shape = 18, colour = mist) +
  labs(x = "Speaking style", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Three levels, two coefficients

```{r}
m_style <- lm(duration ~ style, data = styles)
coef(m_style)
```

. . .

The intercept is the mean of `casual`, the reference level. `styleclear` is clear minus casual, and `styleloud` is loud minus casual.

. . .

A predictor with `k` levels gets `k − 1` coefficients: each level against the reference.

## Three levels, visually

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.0
style_means <- styles |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), .by = style)
casual_mean <- style_means$mean[style_means$style == "casual"]
ggplot(styles, aes(x = style, y = duration, colour = style)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.35, size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = casual_mean, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(data = filter(style_means, style != "casual"),
               aes(x = style, xend = style, y = casual_mean, yend = mean),
               colour = mist, linewidth = 1.2, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))) +
  geom_point(data = style_means, aes(y = mean), colour = mist, size = 5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = casual_mean - 6, label = "intercept", colour = mist, hjust = 0, size = 5) +
  labs(x = "Speaking style", y = "Vowel duration (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Each arrow is one coefficient: how far clear and loud speech lie from casual speech, the dashed line.

## Behind the scenes {.smaller}

R creates one dummy variable per non-reference level:

```{r}
model.matrix(~ style, data = styles)[c(1, 51, 101), ]
```

. . .

| style | styleclear | styleloud | predicted duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| casual | 0 | 0 | b₀ |
| clear | 1 | 0 | b₀ + b₁ |
| loud | 0 | 1 | b₀ + b₂ |

## What is missing?

The model does not directly compare `clear` with `loud`.

. . .

Change the reference level to get that comparison:

```{r}
styles |>
  mutate(style = fct_relevel(style, "clear")) |>
  lm(duration ~ style, data = _) |>
  coef()
```

. . .

`data = _` uses the native pipe's placeholder: the data come from the pipe.

## Sum coding with three levels

```{r}
contrasts(styles$style) <- contr.sum(3)
coef(lm(duration ~ style, data = styles))
```

. . .

The intercept is now the grand mean of the three styles. `style1` is casual's deviation from it and `style2` is clear's. Loud's deviation is not shown, because it is minus the sum of the other two.

## Model fit and assumptions {.smaller}

```{r}
glance(m_style)[, 1:2]
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.8
augment(m_style) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = style, y = .resid, colour = style)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The same assumptions as before. With categories, check that the residuals have a similar spread in every group.

# Mixing predictors

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` mantis shrimp were the first animals shown to see [circularly polarised]{.hl} light. Some species also reflect it from body parts they display in courtship.

_Source: Chiou et al. (2008), Current Biology_
:::

## Categorical and continuous together {.smaller}

Back to Simpson's paradox from lecture 5: F1 by F2 in the formant data.

```{r}
coef(lm(f1 ~ f2, data = formants))
```

. . .

Add `vowel` as a second predictor:

```{r}
m_formants <- lm(f1 ~ f2 + vowel, data = formants)
coef(m_formants)
```

. . .

With vowel in the model, the F2 slope turns positive, as it is within each vowel.

## Three parallel lines

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.2
formants_fit <- augment(m_formants)
ggplot(formants_fit, aes(x = f2, colour = vowel)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = f1), alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = .fitted), linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "F2 (Hz)", y = "F1 (Hz)", colour = "Vowel")
```

The model has one slope for F2 and a different intercept for each vowel, with /i/ as the reference. The lines are parallel, because there is no interaction.

## Reading the mixed model

```{r}
tidy(m_formants)[, 1:2]
```

. . .

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `f2` | `r round(coef(m_formants)["f2"], 2)` Hz of F1 per Hz of F2, within a vowel |
| `vowela` | /a/ has an F1 `r round(coef(m_formants)["vowela"])` Hz higher than /i/ with the same F2 |
| `vowelu` | /u/, `r round(coef(m_formants)["vowelu"])` Hz higher |

## Other coding schemes

Treatment and sum coding are the two you will meet most. There are others, for example:

- [Helmert]{.hl} coding: each level against the mean of the previous levels
- [Successive differences]{.hl}: each level against the previous one, for ordered categories

. . .

All of them give the same fit. They differ only in which comparisons the coefficients show: choose the one that matches your research question.

# Your turn

## Exercises

With `korean_stops` (VOT of three kinds of Korean stops, in ms) and `rhythm_metrics`:

1. Model `vot` by `stop`. Check that the coefficients match the group means.
2. Make `aspirated` the reference level and refit. What changed?
3. Refit with sum coding. What is the intercept now?
4. In `rhythm_metrics`, model `delta_c` by `language` and `rate` (syllables per second) together. Interpret the `rate` coefficient and one language coefficient.

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
coef(lm(vot ~ stop, data = korean_stops))
korean_stops |> summarise(mean = mean(vot), .by = stop)

korean_stops |>
  mutate(stop = fct_relevel(stop, "aspirated")) |>
  lm(vot ~ stop, data = _) |>
  coef()
```

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
stops_sum <- korean_stops
contrasts(stops_sum$stop) <- contr.sum(3)
coef(lm(vot ~ stop, data = stops_sum))

m_rhythm <- lm(delta_c ~ language + rate, data = rhythm_metrics)
coef(m_rhythm)
```

. . .

Each extra syllable per second goes with a `delta_c` `r round(-coef(m_rhythm)["rate"], 1)` ms lower in the same language. Greek has a `delta_c` `r round(-coef(m_rhythm)["languageGreek"], 1)` ms lower than English at the same rate.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- R stores categories as [factors]{.hl}; the first level is the reference
- [Treatment coding]{.hl} compares each level with the reference, and [sum coding]{.hl} compares each with the grand mean
- `k` levels → `k − 1` coefficients; change the reference to see other comparisons
- Categorical and continuous predictors can be combined: one slope, several intercepts
:::
